summary.text: The Qin dynasty was the first imperial dynasty of China, named for the state of Qin, a fief of the Zhou dynasty.
Beginning in 230 BC, Qin conquered the rival states, unified China in 221 BC, and Ying Zheng declared himself Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor.
It lasted only 14 years, the shortest of any major dynasty, but the Han continued its practices, so the Qin are credited as originators of the imperial system.

facts.label: Lifespan
facts.value: 14 years, the shortest of any major dynasty

facts.label: Unification
facts.value: 221 BC, ending the Warring States period

facts.label: Reformer
facts.value: Shang Yang's reforms strengthened Qin in the 4th century BC

facts.label: Standardised
facts.value: Currency, weights, measures and the writing system

items.prompt: Before unification, a trader crossing between states had to adapt to each one's way of doing things. What did Qin's reforms change?

options.label: Each region kept its own system but paid one shared tax
Currency, weights, measures and writing were standardised
Merchants were banned from crossing between regions
Only the writing system changed, while money stayed local

items.explain: The reforms included the standardisation of currency, weights, measures, and the writing system.

items.prompt: After the first emperor died, two advisors put an heir on the throne to exert control. How did that turn out?

options.label: They fought each other, and both died along with the second emperor
They ruled well and extended the dynasty for decades
The heir removed them and restored order
They handed power peacefully to the Han

items.explain: The advisors squabbled, resulting in both of their deaths and that of the second Qin emperor; popular revolt followed and the empire fell.

items.prompt: The Han dynasty kept many Qin military and administrative practices. How does that affect the Qin's place in history?

options.label: The Qin are remembered as a failed state with no lasting effect
The Qin are credited with founding the Han line of rulers
The Qin are credited as originators of an imperial system that lasted until 1911
The Qin are credited only with building the Great Wall

items.explain: Because the Han largely continued Qin practices, the Qin have been credited as the originators of the Chinese imperial system that endured in some form until 1911.

items.prompt: Qin's capital Xianyang was the only capital of its time that needed no walls. What about the surrounding homeland helps explain it?

options.label: The flat open Yangtze valley blocked attackers
A broad moat ran along the Wei River
Peace treaties covered all rival states
Mountains made the Guanzhong a natural stronghold

items.explain: The Guanzhong offered a strategic position protected by mountains that made it a natural stronghold, and Xianyang was the only capital that did not require walls.

items.prompt: Duke Xiang of Song once let an enemy army cross a river and form ranks before attacking, and he lost. How did Qin treat that kind of war etiquette?

options.label: It disregarded the tradition and took advantage of enemy weaknesses
It copied the courtesy and won by patience
It obeyed it as a law of Heaven in every battle
It asked the Zhou court to judge each battle

items.explain: Qin engaged in practical and ruthless warfare, disregarding the military tradition and taking advantage of its enemies' weaknesses.

items.prompt: Hundreds of thousands of peasants and convicts labored under the Qin central government. Which projects did that labor produce?

options.label: A canal joining two great rivers and a harbor fleet
Linked border walls, a national road system and a vast tomb
Border walls and a complete set of written laws only
A national road system and a fleet for overseas exploration

items.explain: The labor enabled the connection of northern walls that became the Great Wall, a large national road system, and the Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang with its Terracotta Army.

paragraphs.heading: China's first empire
paragraphs.text: The Qin dynasty was the first imperial dynasty of China. It took its name from the state of Qin, which was a fief of the Zhou dynasty. From 230 BC, Qin's king, Ying Zheng, fought a string of wars and conquered every rival state that had once sworn loyalty to the Zhou. This ended in 221 BC with China unified. Ying Zheng then named himself Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China, and the Warring States period came to an end.

paragraphs.heading: Short-lived but lasting
paragraphs.text: The dynasty fell apart in 206 BC, a few years after Qin Shi Huang died. It lasted just 14 years and had only two emperors, the shortest run of any major Chinese dynasty. Yet the Han dynasty that came after kept most of Qin's military and government methods. For that reason the Qin are credited with starting the Chinese imperial system, which survived in some form until the Xinhai Revolution in 1911.

paragraphs.heading: From minor state to power
paragraphs.text: For its first few centuries Qin was a minor power. Its strength grew sharply in the 4th century BC, largely thanks to reforms of government and the army led by Shang Yang between 359 and 338 BC. The reforms aimed at a strong central state and a big army backed by a steady economy. Shang Yang himself was executed in 338 BC by King Huiwen, who held a personal grudge against him from his youth.

paragraphs.heading: One standard for everything
paragraphs.text: The Qin made currency, weights, measures and writing the same everywhere, and brought in new weapons, transport and battle tactics. The central government weakened nobles and landowners and dealt with peasants, the great majority of people, directly. That let it put hundreds of thousands of peasants and convicts to work on huge projects. They joined up walls along the northern border that would one day become the Great Wall, built a national road system, and raised Qin Shi Huang's city-sized tomb, watched over by the life-sized Terracotta Army.

paragraphs.heading: A natural stronghold
paragraphs.text: Qin's army was large and efficient, with able generals, and it was better than the other states' armies in both ideas and practice. Unlike many rivals, it used the latest weapons and transport, which helped it move across very different kinds of land. Its home region, the Guanzhong, had rich farmland and was ringed by mountains that made it easy to defend. Xianyang, the Qin capital, was the only capital in China at the time that needed no walls around it.

paragraphs.heading: Breaking the old rules
paragraphs.text: In the earlier Spring and Autumn period, war was treated as a gentleman's activity with rules thought to come from Heaven. Duke Xiang of Song once refused to attack Chu troops while they were crossing a river. He let them cross and form up, and then he was badly beaten. The Qin ignored this tradition and struck wherever their enemies were weak.

paragraphs.heading: A rapid fall
paragraphs.text: Qin Shi Huang died in 210 BC, and two of his advisers put an heir on the throne so they could control the state. The two men quarrelled, and the feud led to their own deaths and that of the second emperor. Popular revolt followed, and the weakened empire fell to the Chu generals Xiang Yu and Liu Bang. Liu Bang went on to found the Han dynasty.
